subtype: Approach: adapting to the mentee's style and background [Revision]
passage: I'm Joseph, and I mentored Rajni for a year. Rajni was the first in the family to finish college, and in our early meetings I'd ask, 'Any questions?' and get, 'No, sir, all clear.' Then Rajni's work would come back with the same doubts, unasked. Around the fourth session I noticed the pattern and realised my plan, with questions put on the spot, suited me and not Rajni. So I changed. I began sending a short note two days before each meeting with the topics, and Rajni wrote questions back on paper. In the room I left a few quiet minutes with nothing to say. The first question that came out of that silence was a real one, about how to ask for feedback. Others kept coming.

qa.q: Around which session did Joseph notice the pattern?
qa.a: Joseph noticed it around the fourth session.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when the same doubts came back unasked?
qa.a: Joseph was puzzled and concerned that the mentoring was not reaching Rajni, which led Joseph to rethink the plan.

qa.q: What other change could Joseph try for Rajni?
qa.a: Joseph could ask how Rajni likes to learn and open a message channel for questions between meetings, since some people find asking in writing easier.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt in the quiet minutes?
qa.a: Rajni probably felt less pressed, having time to think, since the first real question came out of that silence.

grounding: Shows a mentor noticing that a shy first-generation graduate does not ask questions, and switching to written notes before meetings and quiet time.

subtype: Approach: adapting to the mentee's style and background [Revision]
passage: I'm Ankita, and I sat near Vishal the year he mentored Sagar, a first-generation graduate who had joined from a small-town college. In their first meetings, Vishal did most of the talking and kept asking, 'Any questions?' Sagar always said no, and then I'd see him searching the same topic online for an hour afterwards. After the third meeting Vishal changed things. He started sending Sagar a short written note two days before each meeting: what they'd cover, and three questions Sagar could think about. In the meetings, he'd ask something and then just wait, sometimes for a long while, without filling the silence. By the second month, Sagar was bringing written questions of his own. I don't know what Vishal was thinking when he changed his style. But he stopped saying 'Any questions?'

qa.q: What did Vishal send Sagar two days before each meeting?
qa.a: A short written note of what they'd cover and three questions to think about.

qa.q: What might Sagar have been feeling in the first meetings?
qa.a: Sagar was probably shy and hesitant, worried about looking unprepared, so he said no and searched alone later.

qa.q: Why did the written notes and silences work better than 'Any questions?'
qa.a: They gave Sagar time to prepare and space to speak, suiting his style instead of expecting instant questions.

qa.q: How does Ankita see Vishal's change?
qa.a: Ankita notices a mentor who adjusted to the person, and sees it working as Sagar starts bringing questions.

grounding: It shows a colleague watching a mentor notice a first-generation graduate is shy, switch to written notes before meetings and allow quiet time.

subtype: Approach: adapting to the mentee's style and background [Revision]
passage:
Week one. Chetan meets Ishita, his new mentee, a first-generation graduate from a village near Sangli. He talks for forty minutes about system design. She nods and says, 'Clear, sir.' Later, her lead tells him she's struggling with the basics.
Week three. Chetan notices she never asks anything in front of others. So he changes the plan. Two days before each meeting, he sends her a short note: the topic, a small example, and 'write down anything unclear, however small'. In meetings he asks a question and waits, counting silently to ten.
Week eight. Ishita arrives with a page of questions in her neat handwriting, the first one starting 'This might be silly, but'. None of them are silly. Chetan answers each one. At the end she asks, 'Can we do this again Thursday?'

qa.q: What did Ishita say in week one?
What does 'This might be silly, but' suggest Ishita still feels?
qa.a: It suggests Ishita still feels a little shy and unsure, but now safe enough to ask.

qa.q: What else could Chetan do to keep adapting?
qa.a: He could ask Ishita which format helps most, notes, examples or calls, and keep adjusting as her confidence grows.

qa.q: How might Ishita's lead see the change by week eight?
qa.a: The lead would likely see her basics improving and more willingness to ask, easing the worry from week one.

grounding: It shows a mentor noticing a first-generation graduate is shy about asking, switching to written notes before meetings and allowing quiet time.
